ClickHouse

Source: vignettes/clickhouse.Rmd
clickhouse.Rmd

ClickHouse is a SQL database for analytics. This guide uses a service configured to accept OAuth JWT access tokens. Run SQL against a JWT-enabled ClickHouse service using each visitor’s account. The client uses ClickHouse’s HTTPS interface and returns data frames without an ODBC or native ClickHouse driver.

Try the guided demo

Run shinyOAuthDB::oauth_db_cloud_demo("clickhouse") in your R console. This guided example uses Microsoft Entra as the custom JWT issuer. It first asks whether your qualifying Cloud service already trusts that issuer and maps its audience and role claims. Choose Not ready yet to save a draft and get setup links, then resume with jwt_ready = "yes" when configured.

The remaining settings are url (HTTPS database query endpoint), tenant_id, accepted API resource, full delegated scope and Shiny client_id. The API resource’s token version, issuer, audience and role values must match the service configuration. With Entra v2 access tokens, configure the resource API to issue v2 tokens; its App ID URI and token audience can differ. Your administrators should verify the mapping.

Install processx, jsonlite and askpass; no database driver is needed. A confidential client uses masked input or OAUTHDB_CLICKHOUSE_CLIENT_SECRET. The local editable app waits for Run example query and leaves the Cloud service running when stopped. An optional database selects a default for later table queries. See Guided cloud demos.

A standard trial or built-in clickhouse-client --login does not establish this custom-provider flow. Check the documented availability before arranging an account for this demo. Other OIDC providers can use the manual example below; their client configuration differs from this guide.

Prepare a JWT-enabled service

Custom identity providers need a qualifying ClickHouse Cloud Enterprise service. An ordinary ClickHouse Docker container doesn’t supply this authentication feature. The service configuration follows the app.

Setting Where to find it
OAUTHDB_CLICKHOUSE_URL Your service’s Connect dialog, HTTPS endpoint, commonly port 8443
OAUTHDB_CLICKHOUSE_ISSUER The issuer trusted by the service’s JWT settings
Client ID and secret Your Shiny registration with that identity provider
Database roles Existing ClickHouse roles mapped from the token’s role claims

Save the OAUTHDB_* values in .Renviron and restart R. You need no additional R database driver.

Complete Shiny app 

library(shiny)
library(shinyOAuth)
library(shinyOAuthDB)

provider <- oauth_provider_oidc_discover(
  issuer = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLICKHOUSE_ISSUER")
)
client <- oauth_client(
  provider,
  client_id = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID"),
  client_secret = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET"),
  redirect_uri = "http://localhost:8100",
  scopes = c("openid", "profile", "email", "offline_access")
)

ui <- oauth_ui(
  fluidPage(
    actionButton("login", "Sign in"),
    actionButton("logout", "Sign out"),
    tableOutput("rows")
  ),
  id = "auth",
  client = client
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  auth <- oauth_module_server("auth", client, auto_redirect = FALSE)
  observeEvent(input$login, auth$request_login())
  observeEvent(input$logout, auth$logout())
  clickhouse <- oauth_db_clickhouse_api(
    auth$connection,
    url = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLICKHOUSE_URL")
  )
  output$rows <- renderTable({
    clickhouse$query(
      "SELECT currentUser() AS database_user, version() AS server_version"
    )
  })
}

runApp(
  shinyApp(ui, server, uiPattern = ".*"),
  port = 8100,
  launch.browser = FALSE
)

# Open the app in your regular browser at http://localhost:8100
# (viewers in RStudio/Positron/etc. cannot perform necessary redirects)

Save the example as example.R and run source("example.R"). Set database when creating the API client to choose a default database. Use target for a named shinyOAuth token target, and ca_bundle for a private certificate authority supported by your curl TLS backend.

Enable service JWT authentication

Custom identity providers currently require ClickHouse Cloud Enterprise and service version 26.4 or later, or 26.8 for EC signing keys. Configure the trusted issuer, audience, and public HTTPS JWKS endpoint in the service’s JWT authentication settings. Map the provider’s roles claim to roles that exist in ClickHouse, and grant those roles the required database permissions. See JWT authentication and availability.

Use the database’s HTTPS query endpoint, commonly port 8443. A Cloud management API key, database password, or the fact that a server speaks ClickHouse SQL does not establish JWT database authentication. This helper requires a deployment that accepts the visitor’s bearer access token.

Register your Shiny app with the trusted identity provider, using http://localhost:8100 for the local redirect URI. Configure the audience, scopes, and role claims that ClickHouse expects. The example assumes the provider issues the intended JWT access token through its normal authorization-code flow; it does not invoke clickhouse-client --login.

Set OAUTHDB_CLICKHOUSE_ISSUER, OAUTHDB_CLICKHOUSE_URL, OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID, and OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET in your environment.

Native typed parameters

SQL goes in the POST body. Parameter values are supplied separately through ClickHouse’s param_ mechanism and are never interpolated into SQL.

rows <- clickhouse$query(
  "SELECT id, total FROM reporting.orders WHERE country = {country:String} AND id > {after:UInt64} LIMIT 20",
  parameters = list(country = "NL", after = "9007199254740993")
)
day <- clickhouse$query(
  "SELECT {day:Date} AS day",
  parameters = list(day = as.Date("2026-11-03"))
)
at <- as.POSIXct("2026-11-03 12:00:00", tz = "Europe/Amsterdam")
times <- clickhouse$query(
  "SELECT {at:DateTime('UTC')} AS at, {precise:DateTime64(6, 'UTC')} AS precise",
  parameters = list(at = at, precise = at + 0.125)
)

Supply one R scalar per parameter. Missing values use the native nullable representation; declare a compatible Nullable(...) type in SQL. Supply large integers and exact decimals as strings.

POSIXct values are formatted as UTC wall-clock strings, regardless of their R display timezone. Use DateTime('UTC') for whole seconds and DateTime64(6, 'UTC') for fractional seconds; encoding retains up to six fractional digits. Always specify 'UTC' in the SQL placeholder. An unqualified type uses the server or session timezone, and a different timezone annotation changes the instant represented by the formatted string. In the example, noon in Amsterdam becomes 11:00:00 UTC.

Array and tuple parameters use native ClickHouse literal strings wrapped in I(), such as parameters = list(ids = I("[1,2,3]")). I() preserves a value already encoded in ClickHouse’s escaped format; it remains a bound HTTP parameter and is never interpolated into SQL.

Results and statements

The client requests JSONCompact, which retains column order and duplicate column names. Omit FORMAT clauses and output-format overrides from your SQL. Integers of 64 bits or more and decimals remain strings; smaller integers and floats become R numbers. Dates become Date, timestamps keep their server string representation, and complex values become list columns. Empty queries preserve their column metadata.

result <- clickhouse$query(
  "SELECT count() AS rows FROM reporting.orders",
  raw = TRUE
)
result$meta
result$statistics

clickhouse$execute(
  "INSERT INTO reporting.reviewed_orders (id) VALUES ({id:UInt64})",
  parameters = list(id = "9007199254740993")
)

execute() invisibly returns the httr2 response for successful statements. All requests obtain a current token for the authorization that started them. Authorization changes discard late responses. SQL requests never retry automatically, including after HTTP 401, because a statement may already have executed. Redirects are rejected.

Response buffering and complete JSON parsing prevent returning partial rows after a server exception. Operations collect results in R memory. A timeout or sign-out does not guarantee cancellation of a submitted query. Configure query limits in ClickHouse for long-running work. See the HTTP interface.
